units.objective: Understand prices and quantities in everyday errands.

concepts.title: First words and greetings
concepts.explanation: Portuguese greets by the hour, but one word here behaves differently from every language around it: obrigado is not fixed. A man says obrigado and a woman says obrigada, because the word agrees with the person speaking rather than the person being thanked. Get that right on day one and you will sound like yourself rather than like a phrasebook.
concepts.commonError: Say olá the moment you arrive. Men say obrigado and women say obrigada; day-zero learners are understood either way.

concepts.title: Introducing yourself
concepts.explanation: Portuguese says Meu nome é Ana. The é is a word in its own right: é means 'is', and dropping the accent leaves e, 'and'. Sou Ana is the other introduction and needs no eu, because the verb already carries the person.
concepts.commonError: Keep é in Meu nome é Ana. The accent belongs to the word é (is); e without an accent means and.

concepts.title: Polite café requests
concepts.explanation: Portuguese asks politely with Eu gostaria de, and de must stay between the verb and the drink: gostaria de um café. The eu is optional because the verb already carries the person. Thanks agrees with the speaker — obrigado for a man, obrigada for a woman.

examples.target: Eu gostaria de um café, por favor.
examples.meaning: I would like a coffee, please.

examples.target: Eu gostaria de um chá, por favor.
examples.meaning: I would like a tea, please.

concepts.commonError: Keep de after gostaria: gostaria de um café. Chá means tea and keeps its accent.

concepts.title: Numbers and quantities
concepts.explanation: In Brazilian Portuguese the number itself carries gender. Where English says two and stops, Portuguese asks what is being counted: dois cafés but duas maçãs, and you cannot pick the number until you know the noun. Ask a price with quanto custa, which never changes form. Fourteen has two accepted spellings, catorze and quatorze, and both are right.

examples.meaning: How much does a coffee cost?

concepts.commonError: Use duas with maçãs and dois with cafés. Keep quanto custa as one learned price question.

concepts.title: Asking the way
concepts.explanation: Portuguese asks about a place with ficar, literally 'to stay': Onde fica a estação? is the ordinary way to ask where the station is. The directions carry a mark that is easy to miss and impossible to ignore, à esquerda and à direita write their a with a grave accent, because two a's have fused, the preposition a plus the article a. Drop the accent and you lose the 'to' and are left with bare left and right. Desculpe in front softens the question.

examples.meaning: Straight ahead, then to the left.
Excuse me, where is the bathroom?

concepts.commonError: Onde asks where. Quem asks who and o que asks what. Keep the accent on à, which distinguishes to the left from the left.

concepts.title: Prices and paying
concepts.explanation: Portuguese builds the price question on Quanto custa?, and custa stays singular while a single thing is being named. The softened way to order or ask is the imperfect: Eu queria um café, literally I wanted a coffee, is polite where the plain present quero sounds blunt. The bill is a conta, a feminine noun, and por favor completes the request.

examples.meaning: How much does the coffee cost?

concepts.commonError: Não goes before the verb. Portuguese also uses isto for this as a standalone thing, and este before a noun.

concepts.title: Days and times
concepts.explanation: Portuguese numbers its week instead of naming it: domingo is the first feria, so Monday is segunda-feira, the second fair, running through terça, quarta, quinta and sexta-feira. The days are feminine and take na: na segunda-feira. Sábado and domingo are the exceptions, and amanhã (tomorrow) differs from manhã (morning) by one letter.
concepts.commonError: Use na with feminine weekdays: na segunda-feira. The tildes on amanhã and the hyphen in segunda-feira both matter.

concepts.title: Family and people
concepts.explanation: Portuguese keeps the definite article in front of a possessive, which English does not do: a minha família, os meus pais, literally the my family and the my parents. Drop the article and the phrase sounds unfinished. The possessive also agrees in gender with the relative being described, so o meu irmão for a brother and a minha irmã for a sister.

examples.target: Os meus pais vivem em Lisboa.

concepts.commonError: Portuguese keeps the article with a possessive: a minha família, not minha família. It is one of the commonest things learners drop.

vocabulary.example: Eu gostaria de um café, por favor.
Os meus pais vivem em Lisboa.

activities.body: Portuguese introduces you with Meu nome é Ana — 'my name is Ana' — and the little word é carries an accent that matters: é means 'is', while e without the accent means 'and', so Meu nome e Ana would read as 'my name and Ana'. The other introduction is Sou Ana, built on 'to be'. Brazilian Portuguese also lets the subject pronoun go, which is why Sou Ana already says 'I am' with no eu in front of it.

activities.body: The polite request is Eu gostaria de — 'I would like'. What learners drop is the de: it holds the verb and the drink together, and it stays whatever the drink is. Eu gostaria de um café, por favor, and equally Eu gostaria de um chá, por favor. Because gostaria already says who is speaking, Brazilian Portuguese usually lets the eu go without changing the meaning. Thanks is the last thing to get right: a man says obrigado, a woman says obrigada, because the word agrees with the speaker.

activities.feedback: De belongs between gostaria and the drink; without it the request loses the link. Meu nome é Ana is an introduction, not a request.

activities.body: Brazilian Portuguese counts one to ten in two short runs. The number has to agree with what it counts: dois for a masculine café, duas for a feminine maçã, so the noun decides the shape of the number. Quanto custa asks the price and is the same whatever follows it. When fourteen comes up, remember that catorze and quatorze are both accepted spellings of the same word.

activities.feedback: Três is three, and it has no masculine or feminine form to choose between.

activities.feedback: Maçãs is feminine, so the number becomes duas. With a masculine noun such as cafés it would be dois.

activities.body: Portuguese asks where a place is with ficar rather than 'to be': Onde fica o banheiro? The directions are the part to read carefully, because à esquerda and à direita wear a grave accent. That accent fuses two a's, the preposition and the article, and it is the difference between the left and to the left. Desculpe ahead of the question makes it polite.

activities.body: Portuguese does not name its weekdays — it counts them. Domingo, the Lord’s day, is the first of the ferias, and every working day takes its number from there: segunda-feira, the second fair, through terça, quarta, quinta and sexta-feira. They are feminine, so ‘on Monday’ is na segunda-feira, hyphen and all. Sábado keeps the Sabbath’s name instead. And note the pair amanhã (tomorrow) and manhã (morning): a single letter separates them.

activities.prompt: In Lisbon a shop sign swaps a single word at dawn. Choose today's word.
activities.feedback: Hoje is right. What is left over means the week, Monday and tomorrow.

activities.prompt: Predict the sentence before you write it. Monday is the second fair, so count from domingo: today is Monday.
activities.feedback: Hoje é plus the day. Domingo is the first feria, so Monday, the second, is segunda-feira.

activities.prompt: Give the English meaning: Na segunda-feira trabalho.
activities.feedback: Na marks on before a feminine weekday, and segunda-feira is the second fair.

activities.prompt: Portuguese counts the working days from domingo. Counting that way, which day is the fourth?
activities.feedback: Domingo is the first feria; segunda is second, terça third, so the fourth is quarta-feira.

activities.prompt: Read the week. According to the passage, which day opens the week?
activities.feedback: The opening line names it: domingo é o primeiro dia da semana.

activities.prompt: Build the Portuguese sentence for today is Wednesday, keeping the hyphen.
activities.feedback: Hoje first, then é, then the hyphenated day: quarta-feira.

activities.feedback: Manhã is the morning; amanhã, with an a in front, is tomorrow.

activities.body: Portuguese keeps the definite article in front of a possessive, which English does not do: a minha família, os meus pais, literally the my family and the my parents. Leave the article out and the phrase sounds cut short. The possessive agrees in gender with the relative, so o meu irmão for a brother and a minha irmã for a sister.

activities.prompt: Portuguese marks the sister with a tilde. Which of these four words is she?
activities.feedback: The word for sister is irmã, tilde and all; strip its nasal sound and you get irmão, the brother. Pais is the parents, and família the family.

activities.prompt: Irmã is feminine. Which line says I have a sister with the article that matches her?
activities.feedback: Uma irmã is the feminine form; um irmã and uns irmã both mismatch the article to the noun.

activities.prompt: Change the sentence from one sister to two: Tenho uma irmã.
activities.feedback: The plural adds -s to irmã, and uma becomes duas: Tenho duas irmãs.

activities.prompt: Read the family note. In which city did the parents stay?
activities.feedback: The brother and sister have moved on; the parents are the ones still in Lisbon.

activities.prompt: Write the plural word for parents, article and all, into the gap: Os meus ___ vivem em Lisboa.
activities.feedback: Pais is plural and still keeps the article os alongside the possessive meus.

segments.text: Write the plural word for parents, article and all, into the gap: Os meus

activities.prompt: Predict the form before you write it: I have a brother. (ter is irregular in the I form.)
activities.feedback: Ter is irregular, so the I form is tenho and not tene: Tenho um irmão.

activities.prompt: Put the words in order to say this is my family, keeping the article Portuguese wants.
activities.feedback: Portuguese keeps the article with the possessive, so the sentence is Esta é a minha família.

lessons.title: Prices and paying
lessons.objective: Ask what something costs, keep the price frame singular for one item, and hear why Portuguese orders with a softened verb.

legacyExercises.prompt: One of these lines will get a price out of a shopkeeper in Lisbon. Which one is it?
legacyExercises.explanation: Quanto custa? is the price question: quanto asks how much, and custa is the form of custar that fits one item.

legacyExercises.prompt: The meal is over and you want to pay in a Portuguese restaurant. Ask for the bill.
legacyExercises.explanation: Conta is feminine and takes a, and por favor carries the politeness on its own.

legacyExercises.prompt: You find the price reasonable and want to say as much. Negate «É caro.»
legacyExercises.explanation: Não goes ahead of the verb é, and the tilde on não is part of the word, never an optional flourish.

legacyExercises.prompt: Fill the blank in the question you would put to a stallholder: ___ custa o café?
legacyExercises.explanation: Quanto custa is the frame to memorise, and it stays singular while a single thing is being priced.

legacyExercises.prompt: At a pastelaria counter in Lisbon you want the price of one coffee. Ask it.
legacyExercises.explanation: Custa agrees with the one item, um café, so the question stays in the singular.

legacyExercises.prompt: A shop is asking a fortune for something small. Arrange the words into a sentence that calls it very expensive.
legacyExercises.explanation: Muito stands directly before caro, and isto is Portuguese's standalone 'this', the one used with no noun beside it.

lessons.culturalNote: In Portuguese cafés the bill usually arrives when you ask for it, so a conta, por favor ends the visit.

lessons.title: Days and times
lessons.objective: Count the Portuguese week from domingo and keep the hyphens that hold segunda-feira together.

legacyExercises.prompt: In Lisbon a shop sign swaps a single word at dawn. Choose today's word.
legacyExercises.explanation: Hoje is right. What is left over means the week, Monday and tomorrow.

legacyExercises.prompt: Predict the sentence before you write it. Monday is the second fair, so count from domingo: today is Monday.
legacyExercises.explanation: Hoje é plus the day. Domingo is the first feria, so Monday, the second, is segunda-feira.

legacyExercises.prompt: Give the English meaning: Na segunda-feira trabalho.
legacyExercises.explanation: Na marks on before a feminine weekday, and segunda-feira is the second fair.

legacyExercises.prompt: Portuguese counts the working days from domingo. Counting that way, which day is the fourth?
legacyExercises.explanation: Domingo is the first feria; segunda is second, terça third, so the fourth is quarta-feira.

legacyExercises.prompt: Read the week. According to the passage, which day opens the week?
legacyExercises.explanation: The opening line names it: domingo é o primeiro dia da semana.
legacyExercises.passage: Domingo é o primeiro dia da semana. Na segunda-feira trabalho. Na terça-feira estudo português. Na quarta-feira descanso. Amanhã é quinta-feira.
legacyExercises.translation: Sunday is the first day of the week. On Monday I work. On Tuesday I study Portuguese. On Wednesday I rest. Tomorrow is Thursday.

legacyExercises.prompt: Build the Portuguese sentence for today is Wednesday, keeping the hyphen.
legacyExercises.explanation: Hoje first, then é, then the hyphenated day: quarta-feira.

legacyExercises.prompt: Complete with the noun for the morning, not the word for tomorrow: A ___ está fria.
legacyExercises.explanation: Manhã is the morning; amanhã, with an a in front, is tomorrow.

lessons.culturalNote: The numbered weekdays come from the church calendar, where Sunday was the first fair and Monday the second.

lessons.title: Family and people
lessons.objective: Introduce your relatives, and keep the small article Portuguese plants in front of a possessive.

legacyExercises.prompt: Portuguese marks the sister with a tilde. Which of these four words is she?
legacyExercises.explanation: The word for sister is irmã, tilde and all; strip its nasal sound and you get irmão, the brother. Pais is the parents, and família the family.

legacyExercises.prompt: Irmã is feminine. Which line says I have a sister with the article that matches her?
legacyExercises.explanation: Uma irmã is the feminine form; um irmã and uns irmã both mismatch the article to the noun.

legacyExercises.prompt: Change the sentence from one sister to two: Tenho uma irmã.
legacyExercises.explanation: The plural adds -s to irmã, and uma becomes duas: Tenho duas irmãs.

legacyExercises.prompt: Read the family note. In which city did the parents stay?
legacyExercises.explanation: The brother and sister have moved on; the parents are the ones still in Lisbon.
legacyExercises.passage: Somos quatro em casa, mas só eu e a minha irmã vivemos no Porto. O meu irmão Max mudou-se para Coimbra no ano passado. Os meus pais ficaram em Lisboa, na casa antiga.
legacyExercises.translation: There are four of us at home, but only my sister and I live in Porto. My brother Max moved to Coimbra last year. My parents stayed in Lisbon, in the old house.

legacyExercises.prompt: Write the plural word for parents, article and all, into the gap: Os meus ___ vivem em Lisboa.
legacyExercises.explanation: Pais is plural and still keeps the article os alongside the possessive meus.

legacyExercises.prompt: Predict the form before you write it: I have a brother. (ter is irregular in the I form.)
legacyExercises.explanation: Ter is irregular, so the I form is tenho and not tene: Tenho um irmão.

legacyExercises.prompt: Put the words in order to say this is my family, keeping the article Portuguese wants.
legacyExercises.explanation: Portuguese keeps the article with the possessive, so the sentence is Esta é a minha família.

lessons.culturalNote: A família in Portuguese often includes grandparents and cousins, and it is the standard answer to tell me about yourself.
